title: What if ukasar and urapon were the digits of base two?
description: Two Gumulgal words, ukasar and urapon, are used as the two digits of a base two place value system, and six is written with them. The new system is then compared with the Gumulgal number names.
teaching_notes: One idea: in a place value system the position gives each digit its value, so two digits can write every number. Watch for students who read ukasar as two, as the Gumulgal did, instead of as the digit one.

video_script.why: The child uses the base two landmarks and counts from writing nineteen in base two to build a place value system from two words, then compares it with the Gumulgal names.
video_script.substitution: The digits are now the words ukasar and urapon instead of 1 and 0, and the numbers are small.
video_script.anchor: the book's Gumulgal number names, built by counting in twos, and the base two landmarks 1, 2, 4, 8
video_script.payoff_line: With urapon as zero and ukasar as one, six is ukasar ukasar urapon.

final_answer.value: With urapon as 0 and ukasar as 1, for example 6 is ukasar ukasar urapon; the place value version never runs out, while the Gumulgal names add up words and stop at 6
final_answer.spoken: With urapon as zero and ukasar as one, for example six is ukasar ukasar urapon; the place value version never runs out, while the Gumulgal names add up words and stop at six

hold_back: With urapon as 0 and ukasar as 1, for example 6 is ukasar ukasar urapon; the place value version never runs out, while the Gumulgal names add up words and stop at 6
maths_rules: base 2 needs two digits; let urapon be 0 and ukasar be 1; places 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
1 = ukasar; 2 = ukasar urapon; 3 = ukasar ukasar; 4 = ukasar urapon urapon
6 = (1) x 4 + (1) x 2 + (0) x 1, so 6 is ukasar ukasar urapon
Gumulgal names add words (ukasar-ukasar-ukasar for 6, in twos) and stop at 6; anything bigger was called ras
check: ukasar ukasar urapon = 4 + 2 + 0 = 6; 7 = ukasar ukasar ukasar = 4 + 2 + 1
